archetype.name: Rebuilding (first-year regime)
archetype.definition: A new staff inheriting a 3-14 roster that can stop the run and grind clock but can't defend the pass. Injuries are now stripping away the offense it was built around.

report.headline: A run-stuffing defense with no answer through the air, now losing its offense too.
report.take:
Arizona under first-year coach Mike LaFleur is roughly what its record says. The 3-6 mark sits almost exactly on the 2.6 wins the point differential implies, and the -8.6 per-game differential ranks 30th. There's no hidden luck to unwind in either direction. This is a bad team that has picked off a couple of games it had no business winning, beating the Chargers as an 8.5-point underdog and the Rams as a 12.5-point underdog. It has also been run off the field by the better offenses on its schedule.

The defense defines the team, and it splits cleanly in two. Against the run it is genuinely sound: rush EPA allowed ranks 8th and the missed-tackle rate ranks 3rd, so backs rarely get loose. Against the pass it is the worst unit in the league, 32nd in pass EPA allowed. It bleeds on short throws (29th) as well as deep ones (25th) because a 25th-ranked pressure rate gives quarterbacks all day. Yardage hides how bad it is: yards allowed rank a middling 17th, but points allowed rank 31st. Offenses finish drives, scoring touchdowns on 70% of red-zone trips. History says this isn't a fluke. The defense ranked 26th in EPA allowed last year and 31st in 2023.

The offense was the part holding things together, and it is coming apart. Under Jacoby Brissett it was ordinary rather than broken: 20th in EPA, 12th in success rate, 4th in time of possession, and 3rd in short-yardage conversions. That profile leaned on a ball-control, keep-it-close formula. Now the second-leading target, Michael Wilson, is out for the season with a neck fracture. Kendrick Bourne is on IR. Gardner Minshew, who started Week 9, is likely headed for season-ending elbow surgery. Three backs and three linemen, including the center, are on the report. The 3-17 loss at Seattle in Minshew's start is a preview of what this offense looks like thinned out.

From here the schedule is the main reason for optimism. Five of the last seven opponents carry losing records and bottom-half defenses. The question is whether a depleted offense can still score enough to exploit that. Expect more of the same: clock-heavy games, a defense that holds up on the ground and leaks through the air, and a win total that finishes in the same neighborhood as last year's.

strengths.title: Run defense that tackles
strengths.body: Arizona stuffs the run and finishes plays. Rush EPA allowed ranks 8th, explosive runs allowed rank 10th, and the missed-tackle rate is 3rd-best in the league. This comes from sound fits and tackling, not scheme gimmicks, so it should hold. Its value is capped, though, because opponents can simply throw on this defense instead.

strengths.title: Ball control and short yardage
strengths.body: The offense owns the clock, 4th in time of possession, and converts short-yardage downs at the 3rd-best rate while going for it aggressively on fourth down. That shrinks games and explains how an outmanned team stole wins over the Chargers and Rams. It depends on staying on schedule, though, and injuries to the line and backfield put that at risk.

concerns.title: League-worst pass defense
concerns.body: Pass EPA allowed ranks dead last, and the damage comes everywhere: short throws 29th, deep shots 25th. The root is a pass rush that ranks 25th in pressure rate, which leaves the coverage exposed for too long. Last year's defense ranked 26th in EPA allowed, so this is structural and won't fix itself midseason.

concerns.title: Offense gutted by injuries
concerns.body: Wilson (88 targets) is out for the year, Bourne is on IR, and Minshew likely needs season-ending surgery. The line is missing its center to a concussion plus a guard and a tackle. A passing game that already ranked 23rd in EPA behind a line allowing the 27th-ranked pressure rate is now down to Trey McBride and spare parts. The Week 9 three-point output at Seattle shows the floor.

concerns.title: Red zone and takeaways
concerns.body: The gap between 17th in yards allowed and 31st in points allowed is explained in the red zone, where opponents score touchdowns 70% of the time. The defense also rarely flips possessions, ranking 29th in takeaways. Without stops near the goal line or turnovers, a defense that bends simply breaks.

trend.note: The results have swung between upset wins and lopsided losses all year. The late picture is worse than the season line: the Week 9 loss at Seattle produced three points and 50 rushing yards, and the injury report has since added a season-ending loss at receiver and at quarterback.

nextGame.headline: Rams' banged-up secondary is Arizona's only real opening at home
nextGame.body:
The Rams are better than their 5-4 record. They rank 5th in net EPA and 4th on defense, and they are almost a win under what their point differential implies. Their offense passes more than expected (4th in pass rate over expected) behind a line that allows the league's lowest pressure rate. That is a direct hit on Arizona's last-ranked pass defense and its weak rush. Arizona did win the first meeting 18-16 in Los Angeles as a 12.5-point underdog, and the Book again has the Rams by 9.5 with a low 40.5 total.

Availability cuts both ways. Arizona's quarterback situation is unsettled: Minshew is doubtful with a likely torn UCL, and the dossier doesn't confirm who starts. The Cardinals are also without Wilson and Bourne, center Froholdt is in concussion protocol, and guard Gaines and tackle Williams are out. Allgeier is the only healthy back of note with Love, Conner and Knight unavailable. The Rams are thin too. Starting corner Trent McDuffie is out and Jaylen Watson is on IR, Puka Nacua is doubtful, guard Steve Avila is questionable, and long snapper Joe Cardona is out on a special-teams unit that already ranks 30th.

waysToWin.title: Attack the depleted Rams secondary
waysToWin.body: With McDuffie out and Watson on IR, the Rams are down two corners. Their pass rush ranks 27th in pressure rate and 31st in hit rate, so even a backup quarterback should have time. Their weakest spot by role has been the third receiver, who has scored well above his usual output against them. Spreading the ball beyond McBride to whoever lines up in the slot is the cleanest path to points.

waysToWin.title: Replay the Week 6 rock fight
waysToWin.body: Arizona won the first meeting 18-16 by keeping it low-scoring and close. Its time-of-possession edge and the Rams' struggles in one-score games (a 0.4 win rate) favor a tight finish. Hidden yardage helps too: the Rams' special teams rank 30th and they're missing their long snapper, so field position and a kick could decide it.

waysToWin.title: Nacua's absence shrinks the threat
waysToWin.body: If Nacua sits, the Rams lose their top receiver against a defense that has actually held opposing WR1s below their averages. A pass-heavy offense with fewer weapons gives Arizona's coverage a rare reprieve. It also lets the defense's tackling show up on short completions.

waysToLose.title: Stafford carves the worst pass defense
waysToLose.body: The Rams throw more than expected and protect better than anyone. Arizona's defense is last in pass EPA allowed and can't generate pressure. Stafford holding the ball is no problem against a rush this weak, and that is the mismatch that decides the game if it plays out.

waysToLose.title: Depleted offense stalls out
waysToLose.body: The Rams' defense ranks 4th in EPA and 4th on third down, and it shuts down deep throws (2nd) and tight ends (4th in EPA allowed to TE1). That takes away McBride, Arizona's last proven target. With an unsettled quarterback and three linemen hurt, the offense could look like the one that scored three points at Seattle.

waysToLose.title: Red-zone drives end in touchdowns
waysToLose.body: Even if Arizona keeps yardage respectable, it has let opponents score touchdowns on 70% of red-zone trips. A Rams offense ranking 5th in success rate will string drives together. Without takeaways to interrupt them, the margin grows quickly.

nextGame.watch: Who takes the snaps for Arizona, and whether that quarterback can find McBride and the slot against a Rams secondary missing two starting corners.

restOfSeason.body:
The schedule after Kansas City is the softest stretch of the year. Washington, Philadelphia, the Jets, New Orleans and Las Vegas all have losing or .500-ish records and bottom-half defenses. That gives a ball-control, run-stopping team chances to steal a couple more wins. Against that is the attrition. Losing Wilson and Minshew for the year leaves a passing game that was already below average with fewer answers, and the line injuries threaten the short-yardage and clock-control formula that kept games close.

The run defense and tackling should hold. The pass defense won't get meaningfully better, since it is the same problem that sank last year's team. The record is already about where the point differential says it should be, so don't expect regression to rescue anything. Something like a 2-3 win finish over the final eight lands them near last season's total, with the Week 18 game against San Francisco a likely loss.
swingFactors: Who starts at quarterback and how long Brissett holds up
Whether the offensive line gets Froholdt and the injured tackles back
How many of the five soft late-season opponents Arizona converts

confidence.note: Nine games of consistent efficiency data, but heavy injuries and a QB change cloud the offense.
